title: Perfectionism vs. the Minimum Viable Game
author: ia-bin
selftext:
Quick note: English isn’t my first language, so I used AI to polish the wording. The development experiences and questions below are my own.

I think I may have a problem with shipping games.

My first game, iaBrick, had its core mechanic working after about two months.

And I mean really working. I had already prototyped the mechanic in MATLAB, checked the solvability side of it, worked through the generation/optimization logic, then learned Swift from scratch and built the iOS version myself.

At that point I probably could have released it.

But it felt too thin.

So I kept adding things.

First I realized the core mechanic could branch into four different gameplay types, not just “easy/medium/hard” parameter changes, but actual rule changes.

Then I thought the image content wasn’t rich enough, so I made 100+ levels with lots of custom image material.

Then player data felt weak, so I added login, profiles, achievements, leaderboards, etc.

Then the reward system felt generic, so I ended up designing a Five-Elements-inspired resource system that basically became another mini-game.

Then the main game felt too simple compared with the reward system, so I added tools and skills that changed the strategy.

Then all those images felt wasted without context, so I added science/literature/history text.

Then the text felt disconnected from the game, so I built a quiz system around it.

Then a fixed question bank felt boring, so I designed an algorithm to generate lots of different questions from a small knowledge base while controlling difficulty.

And somehow a small puzzle game turned into a giant interconnected system.

The original core game took around 2 months.

All the “making it better” took roughly another 10.

And then the real problem started: bugs.

Not just normal bugs, but coupling bugs. Add module B, somehow module A breaks because they share some data or rule in a way I didn’t notice.

AI later helped me fix most of that, and now I rarely see crashes.

But honestly, I got so traumatized by debugging my own spaghetti code that I still haven’t released the iOS version of iaBrick.

Then I built iaReveal with AI doing much more of the implementation.

Its core engine was basically done in about two weeks.

Very few bugs. No major crashes during development.

So naturally I did the exact same thing again.

I added a photo-management system.

Then multiplayer.

Then somehow panorama viewing appeared.

Then panorama interactions.

Then a secondary mechanic around the panorama.

Then I started thinking about how to connect that back into the main game.

And one day I realized: the core game had been done for more than two months and I was still adding stuff.

Worse, I didn’t even know whether players would like the core mechanic yet.

So this time I forced myself to stop and release it.

That got me thinking about a question I genuinely don’t have an answer to:

Perfectionism vs. the Minimum Viable Game — which is actually better for an indie dev?

By “minimum viable game” I don’t mean shipping junk.

I mean the smallest version that honestly shows the core idea, is stable enough for real players, and gives you actual feedback before you spend another year polishing assumptions.

Part of me really admires devs who disappear for years and obsess over one game until it’s exactly right.

But a lot of indie advice says the opposite: make smaller things, ship earlier, learn from players, iterate fast.

iaBrick makes me think I should have shipped earlier.

But a lot of the things that now make iaBrick interesting only exist because I didn’t.

iaReveal makes me think stopping myself was probably the right call.

But maybe six more months would have made it much better.

So yeah, I’m genuinely stuck on this one.

At what point does craftsmanship become overdevelopment?

And at what point does “ship early” become an excuse for shipping something that just needed more work?

comments.author: sevenoutdb
comments.body:
We have a few different version of this saying in English , “Perfect is the enemy of Good”

So the most important thing is that good enough is good enough and you need to ship your game or else you’ll never be finished.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
it is up to your players. as long as your players support you, you can do whatever you want. 

One common pitfall on reddit is that devs give themselves all these random imaginary rules but the biggest issue was really just 1) they made a game and 2) the game can't find any audience.

comments.body: I also got same concerns like you . I have an ıdea of game design . But i cannot reach that level . For now i accept the minimum playable version until the content is complete  .
